notes.front: What is a configuration item (CI)?
notes.back: An aggregation of system components designated for configuration management and treated as a single entity throughout the process.
notes.explanation: NIST's configuration management guide says the configuration item (CI) is identified, labelled and tracked through its life cycle, and is the target of activities such as change control and monitoring.
notes.example: Like a car model's approved parts list managed as one package at the garage, but for a group of servers or an application suite.
notes.evidence: a configuration item (CI) is an aggregation of system components that is designated for configuration management and treated as a single entity throughout the SecCM process. The CI is identified, labeled, and tracked during its life cycle – the CI is the target of many of the activities within SecCM, such as configuration change control and monitoring activities.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-128, Section 2.2.2 Identifying and Implementing Configurations

notes.front: A hosting team runs twelve identical web servers built from one image and wants to manage their configuration together. Can it treat all twelve as a single configuration item?
notes.back: Yes: a group of system components, such as servers with like operating systems, can be designated one configuration item.
notes.choices:
A) No, a CI must be a single physical device
B) No, only documentation can be grouped
C) Only if the servers are in different buildings
D) Yes, a group of like components can be one CI
notes.choicesExplained: A: NIST lists groups of components and even whole systems as CIs. B: documentation is one possible CI, not the only thing that can be grouped. C: location plays no part in NIST's description.
notes.explanation: NIST's guide gives a group of servers with like operating systems as an example of a configuration item.
notes.evidence: A CI may be a specific system component (e.g., server, workstation, router, application), a group of system components (e.g., group of servers with like operating systems,
notes.source: NIST SP 800-128, Section 2.2.2 Identifying and Implementing Configurations

notes.front: Security-focused configuration management has four phases. Which comes after identifying and implementing configurations?
notes.back: Controlling configuration changes (followed by monitoring).
notes.explanation: NIST's guide orders the phases as planning; identifying and implementing configurations; controlling configuration changes; and monitoring.
notes.evidence: organized into four major phases: Planning; Identifying and Implementing Configurations; Controlling Configuration Changes; and Monitoring.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-128, Section 2.2 The Phases of Security-focused Configuration Management

notes.front: Before any baselines exist, a university's security office writes its configuration management policy and sets up the board that will approve changes. Which phase of security-focused configuration management is this?
notes.back: Planning.
notes.choices:
A) Planning
B) Identifying and implementing configurations
C) Controlling configuration changes
D) Monitoring
notes.choicesExplained: B: no configurations are being defined or deployed yet. C: no change is being controlled; the board is only being set up. D: there is nothing deployed to monitor.
notes.explanation: Planning is the first of NIST's four phases, the groundwork done before configurations are identified and implemented.
notes.evidence: organized into four major phases: Planning; Identifying and Implementing Configurations; Controlling Configuration Changes; and Monitoring.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-128, Section 2.2 The Phases of Security-focused Configuration Management

notes.front: Under NIST's configuration change control, on what basis are proposed changes approved or disapproved?
notes.back: With explicit consideration of security and privacy impact analyses.
notes.explanation: The control then has the decisions documented and only the approved changes implemented.
notes.evidence: Review proposed configuration-controlled changes to the system and approve or disapprove such changes with explicit consideration for security and privacy impact analyses; c. Document configuration change decisions associated with the system; d. Implement approved configuration-controlled changes to the system;
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CM-3 Configuration Change Control, p. 125

notes.front: Which kinds of change does NIST's configuration change control cover? Name two.
notes.back: Any two of: baseline configurations; configuration items; operational procedures; component configuration settings; vulnerability remediation; unscheduled or unauthorised changes.
notes.explanation: The discussion lists these, so procedures and fixes pass through change control as well as hardware and software.
notes.evidence: Configuration change control includes changes to baseline configurations, configuration items of systems, operational procedures, configuration settings for system components, remediate vulnerabilities, and unscheduled or unauthorized changes.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CM-3 Configuration Change Control, Discussion, p. 126

notes.front: An operations lead wants to rewrite the nightly backup procedure without a change request, arguing that change control is only for hardware and software. Is she right under NIST's configuration change control?
notes.back: No: configuration change control also covers changes to operational procedures.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, procedures are outside change control
B) No, operational procedures are covered too
C) Yes, if the help desk is told afterwards
D) Only if the procedure mentions a server by name
notes.choicesExplained: A: NIST lists operational procedures among the changes covered. C: telling people afterwards is not a substitute for control. D: the control covers procedures as such, whatever they mention.
notes.explanation: The control's discussion lists operational procedures alongside baselines, configuration items and settings.
notes.evidence: Configuration change control includes changes to baseline configurations, configuration items of systems, operational procedures, configuration settings for system components, remediate vulnerabilities, and unscheduled or unauthorized changes.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CM-3 Configuration Change Control, Discussion, p. 126

notes.front: In security-focused configuration management, which role makes the final determination whether a change is still an acceptable security risk?
notes.back: The authorising official.
notes.explanation: NIST's guide says this official manages or takes part in the CCB for the systems they authorise.
notes.evidence: The AO manages or participates in the CCB for systems s/he authorizes and may provide technical staff to conduct and/or review security impact analyses. The AO coordinates with the Risk Executive (Function) on SecCM issues and makes the final determination whether or not a given change or set of changes continues to be an acceptable security risk.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-128, Section 2.4 SecCM Roles and Responsibilities, p. 26

notes.front: In security-focused configuration management, which role assists the system owner, conducts configuration monitoring and may sit on the CCB?
notes.back: The system security officer.
notes.explanation: NIST's guide gives this officer the reporting and analysis side of configuration monitoring.
notes.evidence: The SSO assists the system owner with implementation of SecCM for the system, conducts configuration monitoring activities (reporting and analysis), and may serve on the CCB.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-128, Section 2.4 SecCM Roles and Responsibilities, p. 26

notes.front: According to NIST's sample CCB charter, what does the CCB do with change requests? Name two.
notes.back: Any two of: requests impact analysis of proposed changes; reviews change requests; makes decisions; communicates decisions to affected groups and individuals.
notes.explanation: Communicating decisions to those affected is listed among the board's own duties.
notes.evidence: The CCB shall request that impact analysis of proposed changes be performed, review change requests, make decisions, and communicate decisions made to affected This publication is available free of charge from: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-128 groups and individuals.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-128, Appendix H Sample Configuration Control Board Charter, p. 93

notes.front: The CCB has reviewed a proposal to open a new remote-access port and the analysis shows some added risk. Under NIST's configuration management roles, who makes the final call on whether the change is still an acceptable security risk?
notes.back: The authorising official.
notes.choices:
A) The system administrator who will make the change
B) The system security officer
C) The authorising official
D) The user who requested the change
notes.choicesExplained: A: administrators implement agreed configurations and help with analyses; they do not accept the risk. B: the security officer assists with configuration management and may sit on the CCB, but does not make the final determination. D: requesters propose changes; they do not decide on risk.
notes.explanation: NIST's guide gives the authorising official the final determination on whether a change continues to be an acceptable security risk.
notes.evidence: makes the final determination whether or not a given change or set of changes continues to be an acceptable security risk.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-128, Section 2.4 SecCM Roles and Responsibilities, p. 26

notes.front: When implementing an approved change, when is it especially important to notify stakeholders such as users, management and the help desk?
notes.back: When the change needs a service interruption or alters the system's functionality.
notes.explanation: NIST's guide adds that where functionality changes, user and help desk training may be required.
notes.evidence: Stakeholders (e.g., users, management, help desk, etc.) are notified about the change, especially if the change implementation requires a service interruption or alters the functionality of the system. In the case of the latter situation, user and help desk training may be required.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-128, Section 3.3.2 Implement Configuration Change Control Process, p. 49

notes.front: An approved change will replace a doctors' surgery's appointment screen with a new layout and take the system offline for an hour on Saturday. What should happen besides making the change?
notes.back: Notify stakeholders such as users, management and the help desk, and consider user and help desk training for the new layout.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, since the CCB has approved it
B) Tell only the system administrator
C) Delay notifying anyone until after the change
D) Notify stakeholders and consider training
notes.choicesExplained: A: approval does not replace telling the people affected. B: users, management and the help desk are all affected. C: an outage is a reason to warn people in advance.
notes.explanation: NIST's guide stresses notice when a change interrupts service or alters functionality, and says the latter may need training.
notes.evidence: Stakeholders (e.g., users, management, help desk, etc.) are notified about the change, especially if the change implementation requires a service interruption or alters the functionality of the system.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-128, Section 3.3.2 Implement Configuration Change Control Process, p. 49

notes.front: What does NIST's configuration change control require for records of configuration-controlled changes and the activities around them?
notes.back: Retain the change records for a set period, and monitor and review the activities associated with those changes.
notes.explanation: Both duties sit in the control itself, alongside documenting decisions and implementing only approved changes.
notes.evidence: Retain records of configuration-controlled changes to the system for [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; f. Monitor and review activities associated with configuration-controlled changes to the system;
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CM-3 Configuration Change Control, p. 126

notes.front: A routine review finds that a database setting was changed last month with no change request behind it. Under NIST's access restrictions for change control, which records should help the investigation?
notes.back: Logs of system accesses associated with applying configuration changes.
notes.choices:
A) The original purchase invoice for the database
B) Logs of system accesses made to apply configuration changes
C) The system's marketing requirements
D) The staff holiday rota
notes.choicesExplained: A: an invoice says nothing about who changed a setting. C: requirements documents do not record changes. D: a rota may help later, but it is not a record of system access.
notes.explanation: NIST says organisations log accesses for applying changes to support after-the-fact actions if they discover unauthorised changes.
notes.evidence: Organizations log system accesses associated with applying configuration changes to ensure that configuration change control is implemented and to support afterthe-fact actions should organizations discover any unauthorized changes.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CM-5(1) Automated Access Enforcement and Audit Records, p. 129

notes.front: Who should conduct a security impact analysis of a proposed change, according to NIST's impact analyses control?
notes.back: Personnel with security or privacy responsibilities who have the skills and technical expertise to analyse the change and its ramifications.
notes.explanation: The control expects them to review plans, policies, design documents and procedures to see how the change might affect the controls.
notes.evidence: Organizational personnel with security or privacy responsibilities conduct impact analyses. Individuals conducting impact analyses possess the necessary skills and technical expertise to analyze the changes to systems as well as the security or privacy ramifications.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CM-4 Impact Analyses, Discussion, p. 128

notes.front: After a system change, what does NIST's verification of controls enhancement require?
notes.back: Verify that the impacted controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended and producing the desired outcome.
notes.explanation: The impact analysis looks ahead before the change; this enhancement checks the affected controls once the change is in.
notes.evidence: After system changes, verify that the impacted controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended, and producing the desired outcome with regard to meeting the security and privacy requirements for the system.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CM-4(2) Verification of Controls, p. 129

notes.front: A team plans to move a payroll system's database to a new server next week. Under NIST's impact analyses control, when must the potential security and privacy impacts be analysed?
notes.back: Before the change is implemented.
notes.choices:
A) Before the change is implemented
B) Only if something goes wrong afterwards
C) At the next annual control assessment
D) After users report problems
notes.choicesExplained: B and D: analysis after the fact cannot inform the decision to approve. C: waiting for the next assessment leaves the change unanalysed when it is made.
notes.explanation: The control requires changes to be analysed for potential security and privacy impacts prior to change implementation.
notes.evidence: Analyze changes to the system to determine potential security and privacy impacts prior to change implementation.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CM-4 Impact Analyses, p. 128

notes.front: When an unscheduled change must be made and there is no time for the normal change control process, what does NIST's guide expect?
notes.back: The change is still managed and controlled, and the CCB reviews it as soon as practical afterwards.
notes.explanation: Organisations include instructions for handling unscheduled changes in their change control procedures.
notes.evidence: When unscheduled changes must be made and time does not allow for following the established configuration change control process, unscheduled changes are still managed and controlled. Organizations include instructions for handling unscheduled changes within the configuration change control procedures
notes.source: NIST SP 800-128, Section 3.3.2 Implement Configuration Change Control Process, p. 50

notes.front: At 2 a.m. an engineer blocks a port on the internet firewall to stop an active attack, with no time to convene the CCB. What should happen next under NIST's guide?
notes.back: The CCB reviews and resolves the unscheduled change as soon as practical afterwards.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, since the attack justified it
B) Reverse the change until the CCB meets
C) The CCB reviews it as soon as practical
D) Record it as a scheduled change dated last week
notes.choicesExplained: A: unscheduled changes are still managed and controlled. B: reversing it would reopen the attack path; the guide calls for review, not undoing. D: backdating falsifies the change record.
notes.explanation: NIST's guide says unscheduled changes are reviewed and resolved by the CCB as soon as practical after they are made.
notes.evidence: Unscheduled changes are reviewed/resolved by the CCB as soon as is practical after unscheduled changes are made.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-128, Section 3.3.2 Implement Configuration Change Control Process, p. 50

notes.front: Security impact analysis versus verification of controls: when does each happen, and what does it look at?
notes.back: Impact analysis comes before the change and predicts its security and privacy impacts; verification comes after and checks the impacted controls work.
notes.explanation: NIST's impact analyses control and its verification enhancement bracket the change: one informs approval, the other confirms the result.
notes.evidence: After system changes, verify that the impacted controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended, and producing the desired outcome
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CM-4 Impact Analyses and CM-4(2), p. 129
